new_statements.quote: Demarcative stress occurs in a fixed position of certain segments in the stream of speech and marks their boundaries. Segments that are thus indicated differ somewhat from words as defined in II.1.2. and will be referred to as phonological words. [...] Simple words constitute phonological words by themselves. Primary stress, [ˊ], occurs fixedly on the second-to-last vowel of the word, and the secondary stress, [ˋ], as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel.
new_statements.citation: Tsukamoto, Akihisa. 1988. The language of Niuafo'ou Island. PhD thesis, Australian National University, Canberra. Part I, ch. 3 'Stress', §3.1.1 (A) 'Demarcative Stress in Simple Words'.
new_statements.locator: p. 43 (PDF p. 57); definitive stress §3.2 pp. 52-56; secondary-stress restrictions p. 44; fast-speech reduction §3.1.2 pp. 49-52; emphatic stress §3.3 pp. 56-58
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate vowel of the phonological word, counting each vowel/mora separately (long vowels count as two: poo [pó:] 'night', kulii [kulí:] 'dog', letioo [lètió:] 'radio'), so it is a penultimate-mora rule of the Tongan type; secondary stress on alternating preceding vowels (pàsikàla, sìokàalafi). Monosyllabic words and monosyllabic affixes never form phonological words on their own but cliticise to a neighbour, so the deictics ni/na, the person determiners ke/ne, the articles te/he and monosyllabic suffixes pull the primary stress one vowel to the right (fale [fále] but fale ni [falé-ni]); bisyllabic affixes carry their own stress. In nominal phrases, definiteness is marked by shifting the primary (and preceding secondary) stress to the last vowel of the phrase-final word ('definitive stress', §3.2, pp. 52-56).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes: 'as a basic rule, every other preceding vowel' (p. 43); it never falls on the second vowel of two identical vowels or of a rising vowel sequence, or on inserted /i/ in loans, in which case it skips to the preceding vowel (p. 44); in fast speech non-phrase-final primary stresses reduce to secondary with a tendency to alternate stronger and weaker stresses (pp. 49-52).
new_statements.exceptions: Definitive stress: phrase-final word of a definite nominal phrase takes stress on its final vowel (fale 'house' vs falé '(the) house', tangata vs tangatá), with the exceptional placement on the emphatic possessive determiner (ta'akú kulii) (pp. 52-56); monosyllabic clitics (deictics ni/na, determiners ke/ne, articles te/he, monosyllabic suffixes) shift stress rightwards (pp. 44-47); reduplicated syllables of Type II are unstressed (p. 48); emphatic (contrastive and intensity) stress with vowel protraction (pp. 56-58).
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' (slow-speech citation forms), explicitly distinguished from the grammatical word: monosyllables and monosyllabic affixes cliticise, bisyllabic affixes and each member of compounds/base-modifier sequences form their own phonological word; the fixed rule is stated for slow speech, with reduction in fast speech described separately; definitive stress is a phrase-level shift.
new_statements.identity_note: Tsukamoto 1988 describes Niuafo'ou (niua1240) as spoken on Niuafo'ou Island and by resettled speakers, based on deliberate speech of informants who consciously avoided Tongan forms (thesis p. 9); he notes heavy Tongan influence in spontaneous speech. No dialect split is described; the stress system is the same type as Tongan (tong1325) including the definitive-stress shift.

sources.locator: p. 43 (PDF p. 57); definitive stress §3.2 pp. 52-56; secondary-stress restrictions p. 44; fast-speech reduction §3.1.2 pp. 49-52; emphatic stress §3.3 pp. 56-58
sources.note: Primary stress fixed on the second-to-last vowel (mora) of the phonological word, secondary stress on every other preceding vowel; monosyllabic deictics/particles/affixes cliticise and shift stress; phrase-final stress shifts to the last vowel to mark definiteness ('definitive stress', as in Tongan); fast-speech reduction and emphatic stress also described (pp. 43-58).
Nothing on stress; cites Tsukamoto 1988, Dye 1980, Biggs 1971, Marck 2000.
